subChunks.title: Parameters, Return Types & Scope
subChunks.hookHtml: A wizard who recites the same incantation word-for-word every time will never rise above apprentice rank. Real mastery means encapsulating power into a reusable formula — something you invoke by name, with different ingredients, each time.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What is a Method?

A method is a named block of code that performs a task. Once defined, it can be called (invoked) any number of times from anywhere in your program. Methods are how Java avoids repetition and organises logic.

public static int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

Reading from left to right: public static are access/scope modifiers (covered with classes). int is the return type — the type of value this method hands back to the caller. add is the method name. (int a, int b) are the parameters — values the caller must provide.

Void Methods

Not every method needs to return a value. Use void to indicate the method does its work and hands nothing back:

public static void greet(String name) {
    System.out.println("Hello, " + name + "!");
}

Calling Methods

int result = add(3, 7);  // result = 10
greet("Lyria");          // prints: Hello, Lyria!

The Call Stack

Every method call pushes a frame onto the call stack — a record of where execution is and what local variables exist. When the method returns, its frame is popped. Variables in a method are local — they vanish when the method ends. Trying to read a local variable from outside the method is a compile error.

Scope

Scope is the region of code where a variable is visible and usable:

  • Local scope: variables declared inside a method — live only while the method runs
  • Block scope: variables declared inside an if, for, or while block — live only inside that block
public static int square(int n) {
    int result = n * n;  // local — only visible here
    return result;
}
// result is not accessible here — compile error

The return Statement

A method with a non-void return type must return a value on every possible code path. The compiler enforces this:

// Compile error: missing return on else branch
public static int abs(int n) {
    if (n >= 0) return n;
    // compiler says: this method might not return a value
}

// Correct:
public static int abs(int n) {
    if (n >= 0) return n;
    return -n;
}

storyBeats.text: The Academy's lower workshops smell of sulphur and pine resin. Senior apprentices are chanting spells with dozens of steps, repeating entire passages verbatim. A red-robed wizard leans in the doorway, watching with visible frustration.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Rhea
storyBeats.text: Look at them. Thirty steps of incantation to light a single candle. If they had to light fifty candles, they'd be here until dawn. This is why we invented methods — named, reusable formulas you invoke once, then call by name forever after.

storyBeats.speaker: A method that calculates spell power
Master Rhea
storyBeats.text: The method signature tells you everything: what type of value comes back (the return type), what name to call it by, and what ingredients it needs (the parameters). The compiler enforces this contract. Try to pass a String where an int is expected and it will refuse to compile.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Rhea
storyBeats.text: Some methods do work but hand nothing back — they are declared void. Others must always produce a value. If your return type is int, the compiler checks that every possible code path through that method contains a return statement. No exceptions.

storyBeats.speaker: Void method and scope
Master Rhea
storyBeats.text: Variables declared inside a method are local. They are born when the method is called and die when it returns. This is called scope. Variables in an if block die at the closing brace of that block. A tighter cage than you might expect — but it prevents variables from leaking across the program and causing chaos.

She flicks her wrist. One of the chanting apprentices blinks, then whispers a single word. The candle lights. 'Thirty steps,' she says, 'collapsed into one call. That is the power of a well-written method.'

learningObjectives: Define a method with correct return type, name, and parameter list
Distinguish between void methods and value-returning methods
Explain local scope and why variables declared inside a method are not accessible outside it
Ensure every code path in a non-void method has a return statement
commonMistakes: Forgetting the return type — the compiler requires it even for void methods
Missing a return statement on a branch — the compiler will catch it, but the error message can be confusing
Trying to access a local variable outside its scope — leads to 'cannot find symbol' compile errors
Confusing parameters (what the method accepts) with arguments (what the caller passes)
assessmentCriteria: Can write a method with one or more parameters and a non-void return type
Can write a void method and explain why it does not use return (or uses return; to exit early)
Can predict compile errors when a local variable is used outside its declaring block
Can identify missing return paths by tracing control flow through if/else branches
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a method is, why we use them, and what 'scope' means for variables inside a method. Use an analogy — perhaps a recipe or a vending machine — to make the concept concrete for a complete beginner.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
The Academy's spell forge needs three utility methods. Implement each one and call them in main:

  1. calcMana(int spellLevel, int duration) — returns int: spellLevel * duration * 5
  2. isAffordable(int manaCost, int manaReserve) — returns boolean: true if manaCost is less than or equal to manaReserve
  3. announce(String spellName, int power) — void: prints "Casting [spellName] — power: [power]"

In main: calculate mana for spellLevel=3, duration=4. Print whether it is affordable given manaReserve=80. Then announce spell name "Frostbolt" with that power value.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Rebuild from scratch — no starter code. Write a class called SpellForge with three methods:

  • public static double powerRatio(int attack, int defence) — returns the ratio as a double: (double) attack / defence
  • public static boolean isCritical(double ratio) — returns true if ratio is greater than 2.0
  • public static void report(String target, double ratio, boolean critical) — prints: "[target]: ratio=[ratio], critical=[critical]"

In main: call powerRatio(15, 5), pass the result to isCritical, then call report with target "Dragon", the ratio, and the critical boolean.

options: The method does not return a value
questions.answer: The method does not return a value
questions.explanation: void means the method performs work but does not hand a value back to the caller. You cannot assign the result of a void method to a variable.

questions.prompt: A local variable declared inside a method can be used anywhere else in the same class.
questions.explanation: Local variables are scoped to the method (or block) in which they are declared. They cease to exist when the method returns. Accessing them from outside causes a compile-time 'cannot find symbol' error.

questions.prompt: Which part of a method signature specifies what type of value the method sends back to the caller?
questions.explanation: The return type (e.g. int, String, void) is written immediately before the method name and declares what type of value the method will produce.

questions.answer: Missing return statement — the compiler cannot guarantee a value is returned when n == 0
questions.explanation: The compiler traces all possible paths: n > 0, n < 0, and n == 0. The last path has no return statement, so the compiler refuses to compile. Fix: add return 0; after the two if-blocks.

questions.prompt: A developer writes a method that takes two ints and should give back the larger. Which is the best implementation?
options: public static int max(int a, int b) { if (a > b) return a; return b; }
public static void max(int a, int b) { System.out.println(a > b ? a : b); }
public static int max(int a, int b) { int result; if (a > b) result = a; else result = b; }
public static int max(int a, int b) { return a; }
questions.answer: public static int max(int a, int b) { if (a > b) return a; return b; }
questions.explanation: Option 1 returns the value — making it composable and testable. Option 2 prints instead of returning — useless if you need the result in a calculation. Option 3 doesn't compile (missing return result;). Option 4 always returns a regardless of b.

subChunks.title: Method Overloading & Early Return
subChunks.hookHtml: A skilled enchanter doesn't have to choose between a ring of fire and a ring of frost — they carry both, and the academy's catalogue decides which to invoke based on what you hand them. In Java, a single method name can accept many different argument types. This is called overloading.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Method Overloading

Two or more methods in the same class can share the same name as long as their parameter lists differ (different types, different counts, or different order). The compiler selects the right version based on what you pass:

public static int area(int side) {
    return side * side;             // square
}
public static int area(int width, int height) {
    return width * height;          // rectangle
}
public static double area(double radius) {
    return Math.PI * radius * radius; // circle
}

area(5);         // calls int, int version → 25
area(4, 6);      // calls int, int version → 24
area(3.0);       // calls double version  → ~28.27

The key constraint: the return type alone is not enough to distinguish overloads. Two methods with the same name and same parameters but different return types will cause a compile error — the compiler cannot decide which to call.

Why Overloading?

Overloading keeps your API clean. You write one verb (area, print, parse) instead of areaOfSquare, areaOfRectangle, areaOfCircle. The Java standard library uses this extensively — System.out.println has ten overloads.

Early Return

A return statement in a void method exits immediately — even if there is more code below. This is called an early return (or guard clause) and is a powerful tool for removing deep nesting:

// Without guard clause — deeply nested
public static void process(String input) {
    if (input != null) {
        if (!input.isEmpty()) {
            System.out.println(input.toUpperCase());
        }
    }
}

// With guard clauses — flat and readable
public static void process(String input) {
    if (input == null) return;
    if (input.isEmpty()) return;
    System.out.println(input.toUpperCase());
}

Guard clauses are preferred in modern Java style. They reduce nesting and make the happy path (normal execution) easier to read.

storyBeats.text: The enchantment catalogue at the Academy's library displays thousands of items — but every ring, amulet, and talisman is catalogued under a single verb: enchant. The archivist explains that context determines which formula is applied.

storyBeats.speaker: Archivist Solen
storyBeats.text: Overloading allows a single name to handle multiple argument shapes. You write enchant(int power) for a basic charm and enchant(int power, String element) for an elemental one. The compiler reads what you pass in and picks the right formula. Elegant.

storyBeats.speaker: Overloaded enchant methods
Archivist Solen
storyBeats.text: The catch: overloads must differ in their parameters — count, types, or both. You cannot overload on return type alone. If two methods have identical parameter lists, they conflict regardless of what they return.

storyBeats.speaker: Archivist Solen
storyBeats.text: Now — early returns. A method that validates before it acts should not pyramid its logic inside nested ifs. Use a guard clause: check for the invalid case and return immediately. The rest of the method can be written flat, as if the invalid case never existed.

storyBeats.speaker: Guard clauses flatten nesting

learningObjectives: Define method overloading and explain what makes two overloads distinct
Write two or more overloaded methods with the same name but different parameter lists
Explain why overloading on return type alone causes a compile error
Use early return (guard clauses) to remove unnecessary nesting
commonMistakes: Thinking return type alone distinguishes overloads — it does not; parameters must differ
Over-overloading: if methods do genuinely different things, give them different names
Forgetting that calling an overloaded method with no arguments causes a 'no suitable method' error if no no-arg overload exists
Avoiding early returns and building deeply nested pyramids — this is a style smell
assessmentCriteria: Can write two overloaded methods that differ in parameter count or type
Can explain why two methods with the same name and same parameters but different return types will not compile
Can refactor a doubly-nested if block into a flat method using guard clauses
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain method overloading — what it is, why it exists, and what the rules are. Then explain guard clauses (early return) and when you would choose them over nested if-statements.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Implement two overloads of a method called describe:

  • describe(String name) — returns "Spell: [name]"
  • describe(String name, int power) — returns "Spell: [name], Power: [power]"

Also implement safeGreet(String name) (void) using a guard clause: if name is null or empty, return immediately without printing. Otherwise print "Greetings, [name]!".

In main: call both describe overloads and print their results. Call safeGreet(null) then safeGreet("Lyria").
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
From scratch, write a class OverloadDemo with:

  • power(int base) — returns base * base
  • power(int base, int exponent) — returns base raised to exponent (use a loop, not Math.pow)
  • printIfPositive(int value) — void, guard clause: if value <= 0, return early. Otherwise print "Positive: [value]"

In main: print power(4), print power(2, 8), call printIfPositive(-3) then printIfPositive(7).

questions.prompt: What determines whether two methods with the same name are valid overloads?
options: They must have different return types
They must have different parameter lists (types, count, or both)
They must be in different classes
They must have different access modifiers
questions.answer: They must have different parameter lists (types, count, or both)
questions.explanation: Overloading is resolved by the compiler based on the argument types provided at the call site. Return type is not part of this resolution — two methods that differ only in return type will cause a compile error.
label(5) matches the int overload; label(5.0) matches the double overload. Each prints the type prefix followed by the value.

questions.prompt: A developer adds this method to a class that already has public static int compute(int a). Will this compile?
questions.answer: No — two methods with identical parameter lists differ only by return type, which is not a valid overload
questions.explanation: Overloads must differ in parameters, not return type. Both methods accept a single int — the compiler cannot tell which to call at a call site like compute(3). This is a compile error.
